welcome.intro: Build a computer starting from a single NAND gate.
welcome.step1: Each level tells you what the chip you build must do.
welcome.step2: Connect pieces on the canvas and press Test.
welcome.step3: If it passes, the chip joins your palette for the next levels.
welcome.sandbox: In Sandbox you can build anything with what you have unlocked.
welcome.progressText: No account needed, and no cookies or analytics. Everything is saved only in this browser. If you clear the site data or switch browser or device, you start over. To take your progress to another browser or device, download it here and load it there.

howTo.title: How to solve a level
howTo.body: 1. Read the goal. Above the canvas is what the chip must do. Pin names look like this: a, and values like this: 1. The level's inputs and outputs are already on the canvas and cannot be deleted. 2. Look at the table. The Table button shows, for each combination of inputs, what your circuit gives and what is expected. Rows in red are the ones still missing. 3. Build the circuit. Drag pieces from Pieces (or click to add them). To connect, drag from an output dot (on the right of a piece) to an input dot (on the left). An input takes a single wire; an output can feed several. 4. Try it by hand. Click an input to switch it between 0 and 1; on a bus, type a number. Green wires carry 1 and grey ones 0. 5. Press Test. Every case is checked. If something fails, a table says which row and what came out. 6. If you get stuck: open Show hint, read the level's Theory or use Step by step to watch the signal move. Every solved level becomes a chip you can use in the next ones.

bit.text: The smallest unit of information: <v>0</v> or <v>1</v>. In a real circuit it is a low or high voltage.

signal.text: A wire carries a value from an output to one or more inputs. On the canvas, green is <v>1</v> and grey is <v>0</v>; the travelling dots show which way it goes.

gate.text: A small circuit that works out an output from its inputs with a fixed rule: NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND.

truthTable.text: The list of every combination of inputs with the output each one gives. With n 1-bit inputs there are 2ⁿ rows.

nand.text: NAND gives <v>0</v> only if all its inputs are <v>1</v>. Any other gate can be built from NAND alone, which is why it is the game's base piece.

combinational.text: A combinational circuit depends only on the current inputs (an adder). A sequential one also depends on what happened before, because it has memory (a counter).

delay.text: A gate takes a moment to change its output. That is why a signal moves gate by gate; Step by step shows that progress.

binary.text: A number written with bits. Each position is worth twice the previous one: 1, 2, 4, 8… So 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

bus.text: Several wires that travel together and carry a number. Split opens it into single bits and Join groups them back. Bit 0 is the one worth 1.

carry.text: What you "carry" to the next column when adding. In binary, 1 + 1 = 10: result <v>0</v> and carry <v>1</v>.

overflow.text: When a result does not fit in the available bits. With 4 bits, 15 + 1 wraps to 0.

twosComplement.text: How computers write negative numbers: −b is NOT b + 1. That way subtracting is adding.

selector.text: A multiplexer picks which of several inputs reaches the output. A decoder turns on a single output given a number. Together they select data and addresses.

feedback.text: An output that goes back, directly or not, to an input of the same circuit. It is what makes remembering possible, and also what can make a circuit oscillate.

oscillation.text: A circuit that never settles, like a NOT wired to itself: its output keeps changing. The status shows it in yellow.

clock.text: A signal that alternates between <v>0</v> and <v>1</v> at a steady pace. It sets the beat for circuits with memory. You can pause it and step with Tick.

edge.text: The instant the clock goes from <v>0</v> to <v>1</v>. Flip-flops only take a new value at that instant.

latch.text: Both store a bit. A latch copies its input while it is enabled; a flip-flop only on the clock's rising edge.

register.text: A group of flip-flops that stores a whole word and changes all at once on a tick, only if its load input allows it.

memory.text: A memory with many numbered words. The address says which one to read or write.

chip.text: A circuit packaged as a single piece with its pins. What is inside stays hidden: only what it does matters. That is how big things are built from small pieces.

pieces.title: Pieces
pieces.intro: The basic pieces. Besides these, every solved level adds its chip to Your chips.

items.INPUT: A value you control with a click (or by typing a number on a bus). It comes out of <pin>out</pin>.
items.OUTPUT: Shows what arrives at <pin>in</pin>. In a level, it is what gets checked when you press Test.
items.NAND: The base gate: <pin>out</pin> is <v>0</v> only if <pin>a</pin> and <pin>b</pin> are <v>1</v>.
items.VCC: Always gives <v>1</v>. Use it to power relays or to hold an input fixed.
items.RELAY: Lets <pin>in</pin> through to the output only while its coil <pin>c</pin> is <v>1</v>.
items.RELAY_NC: The reverse of the relay: lets <pin>in</pin> through only while <pin>c</pin> is <v>0</v>.
items.SPLIT: Opens a bus into its bits: <pin>b0</pin>, <pin>b1</pin>… Pick the width in Bits before adding it.
items.JOIN: The opposite of Split: groups single bits into a bus.
items.CLOCK: Switches between <v>0</v> and <v>1</v> by itself. It is in the Sandbox; in levels with memory, you control <pin>clk</pin>.

items.test: Checks your circuit against every case of the level.
items.showHint: Shows a hint for the level.
items.reset: Puts the level back the way it was at the start.
items.table: Shows the live truth table, with what is expected and what your circuit gives.
items.theory: Opens or closes the level's history and theory.
items.stepMode: Freezes the circuit: when you change an input, the signal waits. Each Step moves it one gate and the wires that changed glow. It is done when the status says stable.
items.pauseClock: Stops the clock; with Tick you switch it by hand, half a cycle at a time.
items.bits: Picks the width (1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 bits) of the Inputs, Outputs, Split and Join you add.
items.export: Downloads the circuit as a JSON file. Import (in the Sandbox) opens it again.
items.share: In Free mode, makes a link with your circuit and its chips; whoever opens it sees what it brings before loading it. A link holds more than 200 pieces, counting the ones inside chips; for something bigger use Export. From there you can also send it to the gallery.
items.gallery: Community circuits, reviewed by hand, to open in Free mode.
items.saveChip: In the Sandbox, saves your circuit as a chip to use inside others.
items.restoreSandbox: In Free mode, goes back once to the circuit you kept before opening a shared one; it replaces what you have now, so save that as a chip first if you want it. Only one is kept, it is not in Download my progress, and Delete my progress deletes it too.
items.fold: The arrows next to Circuitos and Pieces fold each column to give the canvas more room.

RELAY_NAND.name: Relays
RELAY_NAND.goal: Level 0 (optional): build the NAND with relays. A relay lets its input <pin>in</pin> through only while its coil <pin>c</pin> is <v>1</v>; the inverse one, only while it is <v>0</v>.
RELAY_NAND.hint: Two relays in series from the Source give <pin>a</pin> AND <pin>b</pin>; an inverse relay, also from the Source, inverts it.
RELAY_NAND.story: A relay is a switch moved by an electromagnet: when current flows through the coil, a metal blade moves and closes (or opens) the circuit. It is a mechanical logic gate: you can hear it click. In 1937 Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis that relay circuits follow the rules of Boolean algebra. From then on a circuit could be designed with pen and paper, like an equation. Telephone exchanges used thousands of relays to connect calls. The first computers were built with them too: Konrad Zuse's Z3 (1941) had about 2,600 relays and the Harvard Mark I (1944) was electromechanical. Relays are slow (milliseconds per click) and wear out. That is why they were replaced by vacuum tubes and later by transistors, which do the same with no moving parts.

NOT.name: NOT
NOT.goal: Output the opposite of the input: <v>0</v> → <v>1</v> and <v>1</v> → <v>0</v>.
NOT.hint: NAND gives <v>0</v> only when both its inputs are <v>1</v>.
NOT.story: NOT (or inverter) is the simplest gate: it outputs the opposite of what it gets. In a real chip it is two transistors, one connecting the output to ground and the other to the supply. In 1854 George Boole published The Laws of Thought, where he treated logic as algebra with two values: true and false. His NOT is what here means inverting a bit. This game starts from NAND because any other gate can be built from it. Henry Sheffer proved it in 1913, and Charles S. Peirce had noticed it around 1880. Chip factories rely on that idea: a single cell repeated billions of times.

AND.name: AND
AND.goal: The output is <v>1</v> only if <pin>a</pin> and <pin>b</pin> are <v>1</v>.
AND.hint: It is the opposite of a NAND.
AND.story: AND answers "are both things true?". Its output is 1 only when all its inputs are 1. In real life it shows up in any double condition: an industrial press that only comes down if the operator presses two buttons at once (so no hand can be under it), or a door that opens with a card and a PIN. Its name comes from Boolean algebra, where it is written as a multiplication: a · b. With 0 and 1 the multiplication table is the same as AND's. The N in NAND stands for NOT: a NAND is an AND with its output inverted.

OR.name: OR
OR.goal: The output is <v>1</v> if <pin>a</pin>, <pin>b</pin> or both are <v>1</v>.
OR.hint: Invert both inputs before a NAND.
OR.story: OR answers "is at least one true?". Its output is 1 if any of its inputs is 1. It is the inclusive OR: it is also 1 when both inputs are. In everyday language "or" sometimes means one or the other but not both; that is XOR, the next level. Augustus De Morgan, a contemporary of Boole, described the rules that relate AND, OR and NOT. With them any expression can be rewritten using a single kind of gate. In Boole's notation it is written as a sum: a + b, although 1 + 1 gives 1 and not 2.

XOR.name: XOR
XOR.goal: The output is <v>1</v> if <pin>a</pin> and <pin>b</pin> differ.
XOR.hint: It can be done with 4 NANDs.
XOR.story: XOR (exclusive OR) is 1 when its inputs differ. It is a difference detector. It has unique properties: applying the same XOR twice gives back the original value. In 1917 Gilbert Vernam used it to encrypt teletype messages, and it is still at the heart of many modern ciphers. It is also used to detect errors (parity bits) and, above all, to add, as you will see in the next level.

HALF_ADDER.name: Half adder
HALF_ADDER.goal: Add two bits: <pin>sum</pin> is the result and <pin>carry</pin> the carry (<v>1</v> + <v>1</v> = <v>10</v>).
HALF_ADDER.story: Binary has only two digits, so adding one column is easy: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 10 (that is, 0 and carry 1). The half adder does that column: it gives the result bit and the carry. It is called "half" because it gets no carry from a previous column. Look at the table of each output: you already know gates with those tables. Gottfried Leibniz described binary arithmetic in 1703. In 1937 George Stibitz built a 1-bit relay adder on his kitchen table, the "Model K", which led to the relay calculators of Bell Labs.

FULL_ADDER.name: Full adder
FULL_ADDER.goal: Add <pin>a</pin> + <pin>b</pin> + <pin>cin</pin>, the carry coming from the previous column.
FULL_ADDER.hint: Two half adders and an OR.
FULL_ADDER.story: The full adder adds three bits: the two of the column and the carry coming from the previous column. It is what you do when adding by hand, column by column, right to left. The result is still a single bit plus a carry, because the largest case is 1 + 1 + 1 = 11 in binary. It is the piece repeated in any adder: for 32- or 64-bit numbers, 32 or 64 of these are chained, or faster variants of them.

ADDER4.name: 4-bit adder
ADDER4.goal: Add two 4-bit numbers (<pin>a3</pin>..<pin>a0</pin> and <pin>b3</pin>..<pin>b0</pin>) plus <pin>cin</pin>. The result comes out of <pin>s3</pin>..<pin>s0</pin> and the carry left over out of <pin>cout</pin>.
ADDER4.hint: Chain the <pin>cout</pin> of each adder to the <pin>cin</pin> of the next one.
ADDER4.story: Chaining full adders, the carry of each column goes into the next one. This is called a ripple-carry adder. Its weakness is speed: the top bit does not know its result until the carry has gone through every column. With 64 bits that is a lot. Processors use carry-lookahead adders, which work out the carries in parallel with more gates. In the 1960s and 70s a 4-bit adder came in a single chip, like the 74283, and several were combined to build wider adders.

SR_LATCH.name: SR latch
SR_LATCH.goal: Your first memory. The inputs are active at <v>0</v>: <pin>s</pin> = <v>0</v> stores <v>1</v>, <pin>r</pin> = <v>0</v> stores <v>0</v>, and with both at <v>1</v> it remembers. <pin>Q</pin> and <pin>QB</pin> are opposite.
SR_LATCH.hint: Two NANDs that feed each other.
SR_LATCH.story: Until now every circuit was combinational: the output depends only on the inputs at that moment. A latch breaks that rule with a simple idea: wire the outputs back into the inputs. A circuit with feedback can have two stable states and stay in whichever it is in. That is memory: the circuit remembers which input was active last. William Eccles and F. W. Jordan invented this "bistable" circuit in 1918 with vacuum tubes. Computers of the 1940s and 50s kept their registers in tube flip-flops. Having s and r at 0 at the same time is forbidden: it forces both outputs to 1, and when both are released the result depends on which one changes first.

D_LATCH.name: D latch
D_LATCH.goal: While <pin>en</pin> = <v>1</v>, <pin>q</pin> copies <pin>d</pin>; when <pin>en</pin> = <v>0</v>, <pin>q</pin> remembers the last value.
D_LATCH.story: The SR latch has two awkward inputs and a forbidden state. The D latch fixes it: a single data input d and an enable input en. While en is 1 the latch is "transparent": the output follows the input. When en drops to 0, it keeps the last value. The trouble with transparency: if a latch's output feeds, through other circuits, the input of another latch that is open at the same time, the data can go around several times in one cycle. The flip-flop in the next level solves that.

D_FLIPFLOP.name: D flip-flop
D_FLIPFLOP.goal: <pin>q</pin> takes the value of <pin>d</pin> only when <pin>clk</pin> rises from <v>0</v> to <v>1</v>.
D_FLIPFLOP.hint: Two D latches: one open with <pin>clk</pin> = <v>0</v> and the other with <pin>clk</pin> = <v>1</v>.
D_FLIPFLOP.story: A D flip-flop copies its input only at the instant the clock rises from 0 to 1: the rising edge. The rest of the time it ignores the input. That way data moves a single step per cycle, even if the flip-flop's output ends up, through other circuits, back at its own input. This is what makes synchronous design possible: the whole processor moves to the beat of a clock and on every tick each flip-flop takes a new value. A modern processor has billions of transistors and a clock of several gigahertz.

MUX.name: Multiplexer
MUX.goal: Pick one of two inputs: with <pin>sel</pin> = <v>0</v> the output copies <pin>a</pin>, with <pin>sel</pin> = <v>1</v> it copies <pin>b</pin>.
MUX.story: A multiplexer is a selector: depending on sel, it lets a or b through. It is like a railway switch controlled by a signal. It is everywhere inside a processor: it picks which register goes to the ALU, whether the counter's next value is the next number or a jump, or which memory word is read. In telecommunications, multiplexing means sending several signals over one wire by taking turns in time. The principle is the same: a selector that switches between sources.

DMUX.name: Demultiplexer
DMUX.goal: The opposite of the multiplexer: send <pin>in</pin> to output <pin>a</pin> (<pin>sel</pin> = <v>0</v>) or <pin>b</pin> (<pin>sel</pin> = <v>1</v>); the other one stays <v>0</v>.
DMUX.hint: Each output is an AND of <pin>in</pin> with <pin>sel</pin> or with its opposite.
DMUX.story: The demultiplexer does the opposite of the multiplexer: it takes one input and sends it to one of several outputs. The others stay at 0. It is used to distribute: for example, to decide which register gets the order to store. The RAM at the end of the block uses a version of this idea so that only one word is written. Multiplexer and demultiplexer together make a shared link: several sources, one wire, several destinations.

NOT4.name: 4-bit NOT
NOT4.goal: Your first bus: invert the 4 bits of <pin>in</pin>. Split the bus into bits, invert each one and join them back.
NOT4.hint: Split → four NOTs → Join. Pick 4 in Bits before adding Split and Join.
NOT4.story: A bus is a group of wires that travel together and carry a number. Here each bus has 4 bits, so it carries a number from 0 to 15. Split and Join compute nothing: they only spread the bus wires into single bits and group them back. Bit 0 is the least significant (worth 1), bit 3 the most (worth 8). Bus width defines a processor. The Intel 4004 (1971), the first commercial microprocessor, worked with 4-bit words like the ones in this game. Then came 8, 16, 32 and today 64 bits.

MUX4.name: 4-bit multiplexer
MUX4.goal: Like the multiplexer, but with 4-bit numbers: <pin>out</pin> is <pin>a</pin> when <pin>sel</pin> = <v>0</v> and <pin>b</pin> when <pin>sel</pin> = <v>1</v>.
MUX4.hint: One multiplexer per bit, all sharing <pin>sel</pin>.
MUX4.story: Picking between two numbers instead of two bits is the most common operation inside a processor: which register goes into the ALU, whether the counter moves on or jumps, which value is written to memory. One idea keeps coming back in hardware design: what solves 1 bit becomes N bits by repeating it side by side. That is why 64-bit processors are no harder to understand than a 4-bit one: they are just wider.

DECODER.name: Decoder
DECODER.goal: <pin>sel</pin> is a 2-bit number (<v>0</v> to <v>3</v>). Turn on only the output with that number: <pin>y0</pin>, <pin>y1</pin>, <pin>y2</pin> or <pin>y3</pin>.
DECODER.hint: Each output is an AND of the two bits of <pin>sel</pin>, or of their opposites.
DECODER.story: A decoder turns a binary number into "a single line on". With 2 input bits there are 4 outputs, and only the one with the received number is 1. It is the piece that translates addresses: when the processor asks for memory address 2, a decoder turns on row 2 and nothing else. It also decodes instructions, to activate the part of the circuit that belongs to each one. Classic chips like the 74139 (two 2-to-4) and the 74138 (3-to-8) were used to pick which memory chip answered in an 8-bit computer.

INC4.name: Incrementer
INC4.goal: Add <v>1</v> to a 4-bit number. After <v>15</v> it wraps around to <v>0</v>.
INC4.hint: Bit 0 always flips; every following bit is a half adder with the carry from the bit before.
INC4.story: An incrementer always adds 1. It is a simplified adder: since the second number is fixed, each bit needs fewer gates than in a full adder. Its most important use is the program counter: the register that says which instruction to run. After each instruction, the processor moves to the next one by adding 1. Past 15 it wraps to 0, because the carry from the last bit has nowhere to go. That is overflow: the same effect as an odometer going from 99999 to 00000.

ALU4.name: 4-bit ALU
ALU4.goal: The heart of the CPU. <pin>op</pin> picks the operation: <v>0</v> add, <v>1</v> subtract (<pin>a</pin> − <pin>b</pin>), <v>2</v> AND and <v>3</v> OR, bit by bit. <pin>zero</pin> is <v>1</v> when the result is <v>0</v>.
ALU4.hint: a − b is a + NOT b + 1: bit 0 of op can invert b and be that carry-in 1. Bit 1 of op picks arithmetic or logic.
ALU4.story: The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) is the processor's calculator. It takes two numbers and an operation code, and gives back the result. Subtracting needs no new circuit: in two's complement, a − b is a + NOT b + 1. That is how computers represent negative numbers and subtract with the same adder. The zero flag says whether the result was zero. The processor uses it to make decisions: "if a − b is zero, then a and b are equal, jump". In 1970 Texas Instruments released the 74181, a 4-bit ALU in a single chip, and several of them made up the processors of many 1970s minicomputers. John von Neumann had already described in 1945 a computer with an arithmetic unit separate from memory.

BIT.name: Bit
BIT.goal: A 1-bit memory you control: when <pin>clk</pin> rises from <v>0</v> to <v>1</v>, <pin>out</pin> stores <pin>in</pin> if <pin>load</pin> = <v>1</v>; if <pin>load</pin> = <v>0</v>, it keeps what it had.
BIT.hint: A multiplexer picks what goes into the D flip-flop: its own output (keep) or <pin>in</pin> (store).
BIT.story: A 1-bit register stores a value and only changes it when you want: on the clock edge, if load is 1. The D flip-flop from before stores something on every tick, like it or not. The challenge here is that, when load is 0, what it stores is the same value it already had. It is the basic cell of all the memory that follows: registers, counters and RAM.

REGISTER4.name: 4-bit register
REGISTER4.goal: Store a 4-bit number: when <pin>clk</pin> rises and <pin>load</pin> = <v>1</v>, <pin>out</pin> takes the value of <pin>in</pin>.
REGISTER4.hint: One Bit per bit of the bus, all sharing <pin>load</pin> and <pin>clk</pin>.
REGISTER4.story: A register stores a whole word: several bits that change together on the same clock tick. Registers are a processor's fastest memory: they are inside it and are read in a single cycle. The Intel 4004 had 16 4-bit registers; a current processor has dozens of 64-bit registers and wider ones for parallel math. The whole state of the processor at any instant (which instruction is next, which values it is working with) lives in registers like this one.

COUNTER4.name: Counter
COUNTER4.goal: Counts by itself: on every rise of <pin>clk</pin>, <pin>out</pin> adds <v>1</v> (after <v>15</v> it wraps to <v>0</v>). With <pin>load</pin> = <v>1</v> it jumps to <pin>in</pin>, and with <pin>reset</pin> = <v>1</v> it goes back to <v>0</v>. <pin>reset</pin> wins over <pin>load</pin>.
COUNTER4.hint: A register that always stores (its load wired to the Source) the next value: <v>0</v> on <pin>reset</pin>, <pin>in</pin> on <pin>load</pin>, otherwise the count + <v>1</v>. A bus of <v>0</v>s is the opposite of a bus of 1s.
COUNTER4.story: A counter is a register that feeds itself its own value + 1. On every tick it moves on by itself. With load it jumps to a given value and with reset it goes back to zero. That is exactly what the program counter needs: move on instruction by instruction, jump to another part of the program and start from zero at power-up. Outside processors, counters measure time and divide frequencies: a digital wristwatch counts the vibrations of a quartz crystal (32,768 per second) to know when a second has passed. The 74161 chip is a 4-bit counter with load and clear, very much like this one.

RAM4.name: RAM
RAM4.goal: Four 4-bit words. <pin>out</pin> shows the word at address <pin>addr</pin>; when <pin>clk</pin> rises and <pin>load</pin> = <v>1</v>, <pin>in</pin> is stored at that address.
RAM4.hint: Four registers. The decoder decides which one gets <pin>load</pin>, and two levels of multiplexers pick which one is read.
RAM4.story: RAM (random-access memory) holds many words and lets you read or write any of them in the same time, just by giving its address. This RAM is static (SRAM): each bit is a flip-flop, as in a processor's cache. A computer's main memory is dynamic (DRAM): each bit is a tiny capacitor that has to be recharged thousands of times per second, but takes much less space. Before chips, memory was made of cathode-ray tubes (the Williams tube, 1947) and then of ferrite cores, magnetic rings threaded by wires (from 1953). In 1970 Intel released the 1103, the first commercial DRAM chip, which put an end to core memory. With RAM, a counter, registers and an ALU you have the parts of a computer: what is left is wiring them so they read and run a program.
